kan1: Is exercise safe during cancer treatment, does it help fatigue, can you lift weights if you are at risk of lymphoedema? Guidelines, recent trials and six exercises.
kan2: Exercise during and after cancer treatment
kan3: People used to be advised to rest during cancer treatment. Today the guidelines say the opposite: the right dose of exercise reduces fatigue, anxiety and depression and improves physical function and quality of life. In some cancers it may also improve the course of the disease.
kan5: Weekly aerobic and resistance exercise recommended by the guideline
kan6: Studies in the meta-analysis that found exercise more effective than medication for cancer-related fatigue
kan7: Lower risk of cancer returning, a new cancer or death with an exercise programme after colon cancer
kan8: 8-year survival in the exercise group of the same trial (83% in the health education group)
kan10: According to the guideline drawn up by international experts in 2019, exercise during and after cancer treatment reduces fatigue, anxiety and depression, improves physical function and quality of life, and does not worsen lymphoedema. The guideline sets a more achievable target than the 150 minutes a week advised in the past: aerobic and resistance exercise three times a week, for about 30 minutes each time.
kan12: One of the most common complaints of people with cancer is tiredness that does not go away with rest. In a meta-analysis of 113 studies and 11,525 people, exercise and psychological support clearly reduced this fatigue, while the effect of medication was much more limited. The researchers recommend exercise and psychological support as the first choice.
kan13: Can exercise be part of treatment?
kan14: In the CHALLENGE trial of 889 people with colon cancer in 6 countries who had completed chemotherapy, those who took part in a 3-year exercise programme supported by a coach had a 28% lower risk of the cancer returning, a new cancer or death, and a 37% lower risk of death. It is the first large randomised trial to show that exercise can be part of treatment in some cancers.
kan15: There is good news for people at risk of lymphoedema too: in a study of 154 women with breast cancer who had had lymph nodes removed from the armpit, a gradually increased weight-training programme did not increase the risk of lymphoedema; it developed in 11% of the programme group and 17% of the other group.
kan17: Talk to your treatment team before starting an exercise programme. Some adjustments may be needed depending on your treatment, your surgery and your general health.
kan18: Take a break from exercise if you have a fever, an infection or very low blood counts.
kan19: If the cancer has spread to the bone, avoid jumping and high-impact movements, and get specialist help with your programme.
kan20: If you have numbness in your hands or feet, hold on to a support during balance exercises.
kan21: After surgery, follow the time frames and restrictions your surgeon advises.
kan22: On bad days, reduce the time and intensity rather than skipping exercise altogether.

kan32: Sit or stand tall. Without lifting your shoulders, draw your shoulder blades back and down towards each other, hold for 5 seconds and release. Good for posture after chest surgery.
kan34: For most people, yes; the guidelines recommend exercise during treatment too. On days when you feel tired, reduce the time and intensity. If you have a fever or an infection, or your blood counts are very low, take a break from exercise and check with your treatment team.
kan35: I am exhausted. Isn't it better to rest?
kan36: Resting for long periods often makes fatigue worse. In a meta-analysis of 113 studies and 11,525 people, exercise and psychological support were more effective than medication for cancer-related fatigue; the researchers recommend them as the first choice. Start short and gentle and build up slowly.
kan37: I am at risk of lymphoedema. Can I lift weights?
kan38: Weight training that is increased gradually appears to be safe. In a study of 154 women with breast cancer who had had lymph nodes removed from the armpit, lymphoedema developed in 11% of those who took part in a supervised weight-training programme and 17% of those who did not. Start with light weights, with a physiotherapist at first.
kan40: The best option is to combine aerobic exercise such as walking with muscle-strengthening exercises. The guideline recommends aerobic and resistance exercise three times a week, for about 30 minutes each time. If that target feels far away, start with shorter sessions; a little movement is better than none.
kan41: When to stop exercising and get help
kan42: Stop and contact your treatment team if you notice any of these during or after exercise:
kan43: Chest pain, unusual shortness of breath or feeling faint (112)
kan45: Swelling, pain and redness in the calf
kan47: New swelling or a feeling of heaviness in an arm or leg
